title: The Occupation

dialogue.text: You hear them before you open the door. Marić and Dusek. The words are controlled but the temperature is not.
These are workers. Not insurgents. Not criminals. Workers who have been told for eleven days that someone will listen and no one has listened.
They stopped being workers when they occupied the facility. The legal status changed at that moment regardless of the sympathy the situation deserves.
The legal status. Eleven families without income for eleven days and you're talking about legal status.
I'm talking about what I can and cannot do under the law. Which is relevant since you're about to ask me to do something.
They both turn when you enter. The argument doesn't stop — it pauses, which is different.

monologue: Eleven days. Someone planted a garden in the factory courtyard — I read that in Dusek's report, one line buried in the security assessment. Someone brought seeds. That detail keeps coming back to me. People don't plant gardens in places they're about to leave. These workers intend to stay until someone takes them seriously. The question is what taking them seriously actually costs.

choices.text: What are their actual demands? Specifically.
Dusek — what's the security situation on the ground right now?
Gregor — you know these people. What do they actually need to go home?
Vostane — what does this cost per day?

dialogue.text: Three demands. Reinstatement of the twelve workers dismissed last month — the union says without cause, the management says performance. Written guarantee that the Kravenstal plant will not be privatized under the new economic program. And a meeting. A real meeting. With someone who has authority.
That third demand. That's the one that matters. They've been promised meetings before.
The twelve dismissed workers are a labor dispute. The privatization guarantee is a policy commitment. The meeting request is the only one that doesn't bind us to anything we haven't decided.
It binds us to showing up. Which apparently is a commitment this government needs to think about.

choices.text: What's the security situation if we don't act this week?
I want to negotiate. What does that actually look like?
I've heard enough to decide.

dialogue.text: Four hundred and twelve workers. They have been organized and nonviolent for eleven days. Two local police units are on standby — they haven't been deployed because the regional commander made a sensible judgment that deploying them would change the situation rather than resolve it.
The national guard has three companies in Kravenstal for the winter rotation. They could be at the facility in forty minutes.
My assessment: the occupation is stable and nonviolent. Deploying force against a stable nonviolent occupation transforms it into something else. I want that assessment on record.
She's right. The workers are watching to see if this government is different. Force answers that question in a way we can't walk back.

choices.text: What happens if it stays unresolved for another two weeks?
What's the economic cost of continued occupation?
I've heard what I need. My decision.

dialogue.text: Two scenarios. The workers remain organized and the occupation continues — manageable but the economic pressure builds. Or solidarity actions begin at other facilities. Thornfeld has a paper mill that's been watching this closely. Sevagrad has port workers who haven't forgotten their wage dispute from last year.
If this spreads, it is no longer a labor dispute. It becomes a test of the government's authority.
Which means resolving it now, while it's still a labor dispute, is considerably cheaper than resolving it later.
Or we could resolve it because it's the right thing to do. I know that's not the framing in this room.

choices.text: Gregor — what does resolution actually look like?
Decision time.

dialogue.text: I go to Kravenstal. Not an envoy — me. I sit with the union leadership. I tell them the reinstatement decision will go to independent labor arbitration within thirty days, which is what the law requires anyway. I tell them the privatization question is under review and no decision has been made. And I tell them the Chancellor is aware of this situation personally.
That last part matters more than anything else. They need to know someone at the top of this government has heard their names.
A pause. Dusek says nothing. Vostane looks at her figures. Vyktor is watching you.
My father worked that mine.
He says it quietly. Not as an argument. Just as a fact that needs to be in the room.

choices.text: I know, Gregor. That's why I'm asking you.
If your negotiation fails, what's the fallback?

dialogue.text: Three negotiation structures. Send Marić as Labor Minister — credible, personal, but it elevates the dispute to ministerial level which sets a precedent. Send a formal government mediator — procedurally correct, less personal, likely acceptable to both sides. Or offer a direct meeting with the Chancellor's office — highest possible signal, cannot be done for every labor dispute that follows.
The workers don't need a procedure. They need a person.
Every day of the occupation costs fourteen thousand Krone in lost production and security standby costs. That is also a person. Several hundred of them, actually.

choices.text: Send Marić. A person, not a procedure.
Send a formal mediator. Set the right precedent.
I'll go myself.

dialogue.text: Silence. Then Dusek speaks first.
Security arrangements for a Chancellor visit to an active occupation will take forty-eight hours to set up properly.
The press will be there within an hour of the announcement. This becomes the image of the administration's labor policy. Make sure you want that image.
I want that image.

choices.text: I want it too. Set it up.
On reflection — send Marić. I'll follow up personally after the occupation ends.

dialogue.text: Fourteen thousand Krone daily in direct costs. The indirect costs — supply chain disruption, investor confidence, potential solidarity actions — are not calculable with precision. Conservative estimate: the longer this continues, the more expensive every resolution becomes.

I will say one more thing and then I'll stay out of the political argument. The twelve dismissed workers — if their dismissal was without cause, their reinstatement costs nothing. If their dismissal was justified, their reinstatement costs credibility. That distinction should be established before any commitment is made.
Marić looks at her. Something passes across his face — not hostility, but something more complicated.
Their dismissal was without cause. I checked.
Then reinstate them. That costs nothing.

choices.text: Agreed on the reinstatement. Now what about the larger question.
What about the security picture?

dialogue.text: The room waits. Four people around a table. The factory in Kravenstal is four hours north. The garden in the courtyard is probably still growing.
Whatever we decide, we decide it now. The regional commander needs an answer before the morning shift.

final_labor_choice.monologue: Marić's father worked that mine. Dusek's assessment is that force changes the situation rather than resolves it. Vostane says the reinstatement costs nothing if the dismissals were without cause. And someone in Kravenstal planted a garden because they intended to stay. I know what I'm going to decide. I've known since Marić said his father worked that mine. The question is how I say it.

choices.text: Send Marić to negotiate. Reinstate the twelve workers immediately pending arbitration. No privatization decision until the occupation ends. No force deployed.

reactions.text: He nods once. The kind of nod that is holding something back — relief, or the memory of his father, or both.
I'll keep the guard companies on standby. Not deployed. Just ready.
Every day costs fourteen thousand Krone. Make sure Marić is effective.

choices.text: Deploy the national guard. Lawful order to vacate. We enforce the law and deal with the political consequences afterward.

reactions.text: She picks up her radio before you finish speaking.
You're making the same mistake they made in '38.
He watches you. Not with judgment. With the careful attention of a man who is updating his assessment of the administration.

choices.text: Formal government mediator. Offer binding arbitration on all three demands. The occupation suspends pending mediation or police enforce the vacate order.

reactions.text: Clean. Precedent-setting. The press will call it bureaucratic. The Assembly will call it correct.
He looks at his hands. He does not look up for a moment.
I'll stand down the guard companies pending mediation outcome.

choices.text: I'm going to Kravenstal myself. Set up the security. Tell the press. I want to look these workers in the eye.

reactions.text: He stands straighter. Something in his face that you have not seen before.
Forty-eight hours for proper security arrangements. I won't move faster than that.
The press will be there. Make sure you know what you're going to say before you arrive.
